newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium plans to increase gold coin sales.
newsitem.headline: Belgium plans to increase gold coin sales.

text.p: Belgium wants to sell more of its gold reserves in the form of commemorative coins in the coming years according to a government proposal made in parliament this week, central bank officials said on Wednesday. The government has proposed increasing the percentage of the central bank's gold reserves that can be sold as coins to 10 percent of the weight of the reserves held by the bank in 1987 from 2.75 percent at present.
The gold coin sales could reach a maximum two percent of the allowed total a year and would require prior approval by the planned European Central Bank, according to the draft government proposal.
The retention of the 1987 reference date in the proposal is important because Belgium has been one of the world's largest official sellers of reserves in recent years.
At the beginning of 1987 the central bank held 1,329 tonnes of gold but had sold 733 tonnes by the end of last year, cutting its reserve to around 600 tonnes, bank officials said.
Ten percent of the 1987 total would be 133 tonnes.
The National Bank of Belgium (NBB) is at present authorised to sell up to 2.75 percent of its 1987 gold reserve in the form of coins. All the proceeds go to the state.

At the end of 1995 it had used all but 0.73 percent of this facility. In 1996 it did not sell any commemorative coins but is presently selling a number of gold "euros" to mark Europe's single currency plans.
The proposed additional gold coin sales would allow Belgium to cut its massive state debt further, as required under the plans for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Under the draft, the proceeds of the sales would have to be used exclusively towards cutting the debt, which at around 129 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) is the highest in the EU.

The proposal has been made as part of plans to reform the central bank's statutes to bring them into line with the Maastricht Treaty's requirements on central bank independence. However, it is a recent addition. When the draft central bank law was published earlier this year it left the gold coin sale limit unchanged at 2.75 percent.
The proposal must still be adopted by the full Belgian parliament before it would pass into law.

One central bank official said he was not sure when it could then take effect, but noted the ECB, which would have to vet the sales to make sure they were not destabilising, is due to be operational from January 1999.
